newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines boxes with Thailand's shadow.
newsitem.headline: Philippines boxes with Thailand's shadow.

text.p: Asia's newest economic tiger cub, the Philippines, is finding to its frustration that investors are beginning to associate it with some of the grimmer aspects of being in the world's fastest growing region.
The biggest worry now is that problems in the sagging Philippine property market could damage its banks as has happened in Thailand.
But analysts caution against making too quick a comparsion, arguing that Thailand's woes have been a warning to Philippine authorities who have begun to watch their step more carefully.
"The Philippines will not become the next institutional graveyard of Asia," SBC Warburg said in its latest report on the country.

But there have been some uncomfortable moments, highlighted by an almost 15 percent fall in the Philippine stock market index in just over two months. The drop was triggered in part by jitters that any damage to the real estate industry could spill over into the rest of the economy.

"(The comparison with Thailand) is very much overplayed...the central bank seems to be learning from the Thai experience and has decided to put some constraints on loan exposure," said DBS Securities senior economist Al Rillo.

Dharmala Securities economist Manuel Goseco added: "We're beginning to price in the bad news that hasn't happened. It's very frustrating... We're fighting a pessimistic mood which hopefully will be brushed away by the corporate earnings which are coming out."
"But the healthy part of it is that we are taking precautionary measures," he added.
Most economists are sticking to forecasts of fairly robust economic growth this year, although less than the government prediction of up to eight percent gross national product growth.

Last week, the Asian Development Bank said the Philippines finally was in position to match the economic growth rates of its neighbours, who have been booming since the 1980s. But it still must improve the country's infrastructure, stabilise the economy, sort out fiscal problems and keep monetary policy in check.
The trade deficit is one clear danger, analysts said, warning that it threatens to widen even further.
"The country must address this because I don't think we will be able to sustain our growth if the deficit keeps widening," Rillo said.
Many economists are urging the government to let the peso slip further to boost exports.

Also, money is beginning to move into non-productive sectors instead of manufacturing, warned Janet Henry, a Hong Kong-based analyst with James Capel. She pointed to export drops for the key garment and footwear industries.
"I am concerned about the slowdown in manufacturing activity at a time when there is an awful lot of money going into the asset markets," she said.

Analysts also want to see the final tax reforms get through Congress, the last step for the country to free itself of more than 30 years of International Monetary Fund supervision. The IMF is scheduled to relinquish that role on June 30.
